output.headline: Banks’ bumper profits set to help fund Healey’s first budget
output.bodyHtml:
John Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget, to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, the Guardian understands.

Lenders have been logging strong earnings on the back of rising interest rates, with the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group – alone having generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.

Thinktanks and trade unions have repeatedly urged Healey to tax Britain’s banks more heavily, an option considered but rejected by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who was wary of deterring future investment.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), said: ‘Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits, driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.’

The chancellor is in Bangkok, where the International Monetary Fund has praised the UK’s progress towards balancing the books, urging him to ‘stay the course’.

To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, the Guardian understands Healey has decided to tap the financial sector for additional revenue.

One option understood to be under discussion – reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt – would raise upwards of £2bn a year.

Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, Healey praised the banks as crucial to supporting economic growth. ‘People too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects,’ he said.

But he is nevertheless believed to be minded to increase the surcharge banks pay on their profits, over and above corporation tax. Industry figures believe that will probably mean raising the surcharge back to 8%, from 3% at present.

The UK’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as bond markets have responded to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the Middle East conflict.

Analysts have suggested that could as much as halve the £24bn cushion Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules at the time of the spring forecast in March.

Healey is understood to be willing to accept a narrower ‘headroom’, but is also keen to convince bond markets he is wedded to deficit reduction.

Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. UK bosses of lenders including HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and Santander met Healey last week but were given no reassurance that bank tax hikes had been ruled out.

Their lobby groups – including UK Finance and TheCityUK – wrote to Healey days later, saying that on top of ‘weakening investors confidence and damaging UK attractiveness’, higher taxes would force them to move staff and business out of the country.

That echoed warnings by the chief executive of JP Morgan, Jamie Dimon, who said in May he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks. News of the tower – which will house more than half of the US investment bank’s 23,000 UK staff – came days after Reeves spared the sector further tax rises in her 2025 autumn budget.

One industry source said banks were resigned to a rise in the surcharge. They believe Healey is minded to reverse Hunt’s cut – taking it back to 8% – but not go further. Such a move would raise £2.25bn a year, according to analysis by the TUC.

Another industry source said they were caught off guard by the change in messaging, coming just hours after Healey hailed banks as a ‘jewel’ in the crown of the British economy. ‘We’re surprised to see this following earlier comments which appeared to be more supportive of the sector.’

Asked how much the banking industry might be able to absorb in tax rises, the head of policy at TheCityUK, John Godfrey, said banks ‘do not want to get into debating the menu of taxation. The fact is that we don’t want to eat in that restaurant.’

Healey has also been ‘listening to representations’ from specialist banks, including Revolut and Shawbrook, that want the profit threshold at which the surcharge kicks in to be raised from £100m to £500m.

One government source said Labour was mindful of the UK needing to offer a positive environment for startup banks, especially the lending they offered to small businesses.

The TUC has lobbied for a much more punitive increase, to 16%, saying that could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years.

Healey said he wanted his first budget as chancellor to give ‘breathing space’ to both consumers and businesses in the face of rising energy prices.

There will be little additional funding for other Whitehall departments, however, which he stressed would have to stick to the budgets Reeves set out at her spending review in June 2025.

‘It’s important that they do manage within what they’ve got, and it’s part of the job,’ Healey said. ‘You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things, or more.’

The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said Reeves’s plans could result in real-terms spending cuts for some departments in the later years of the spending review period.

Related: UK economy unexpectedly grows in August despite fall in consumer spending

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, used a visit to a financial services firm in Edinburgh on Thursday to caution against further banking tax rises, saying the sector already faced a higher effective tax rate than in many other big global financial centres.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: ‘Britain needs growth. But a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it. Labour should be backing businesses and wealth-creators, not making their lives even harder. Rather than hiking taxes yet again, Labour should cut spending.’

As well as an energy support package for households and businesses, Healey’s first budget is expected to set out more details of plans to devolve income tax to mayoralties, and explain how the government will fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer before he stepped down as prime minister.

Healey is expected to duck the longer-term question of when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence, the issue over which he resigned as defence secretary in June, contributing to Starmer’s downfall.
output.standfirst: Exclusive: Chancellor poised to raise the bank surcharge tax after banks logged bumper profits, as war in the Middle East inflicts damage on the public finances ahead of his first budget.
output.progress: John Healey is planning to raise the bank surcharge tax, tapping banks' bumper profits to help fund his first budget.

context.text: Healey is also reportedly drawing up a tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could raise up to £1bn more for the Treasury.

output.headline: Starlink access restored for Ukraine, Streeting says, as he makes case for US support
output.bodyHtml:
Wes Streeting said he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored for Ukraine’s military, after a dispute earlier in the week had disrupted Kyiv’s war effort.

The defence secretary, who travelled to Washington to urge the US to stand by Ukraine and to cool tensions between the two countries, said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”

The British defence secretary, giving a speech before the meeting with Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity.

Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the dispute over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military.

He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.”

The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries.

Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before meeting Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East.

The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis.

But it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he felt personally betrayed by Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled a version of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine.

Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy.

Developing the theme, Streeting made a direct appeal to the US audience, saying: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together.

“The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”.

Trump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK.

“Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said.

The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable.

It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, and concerns about Ukraine’s ability to intercept new Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities.

Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month.
output.standfirst: Wes Streeting says he has been ‘reassured directly’ by his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, that Ukraine’s Starlink access has been restored, after a sudden restriction on Monday disrupted Kyiv’s war effort
output.progress: Streeting says Hegseth has personally reassured him that Ukraine's Starlink access, restricted since Monday, is now restored.

output.headline: Cross-party and global pressure persuades Trump to call off execution livestream
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump has called off a widely condemned plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

In a social media post on Thursday, Trump said that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device”, after earlier arguing that broadcasting such an execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan”.

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump added. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose.”

Related: Archbishop of US military condemns Pentagon plans to livestream execution

Hasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot by law enforcement officers during the shooting at Fort Hood, now uses a wheelchair.

The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, said last week that the execution of Hasan would be a public event. Hasan’s sentence will be the first military execution in more than 60 years, and would have been the first in US history to be publicly broadcast.

In a statement to the Guardian on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Pentagon said Trump and Hegseth “spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution” before Trump’s statement. Hegesth “supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned”, they added.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice last Thursday, Hegseth said he supported the public execution “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things”.

Many US lawmakers, from across the political spectrum, condemned the announcement and urged Hegseth to reconsider, as the Trump administration faced sweeping criticism, including comparisons to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan.

Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, wrote in a post on social media: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”

In another post, Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said that there was “no need to livestream any execution, including this one”, adding that she “would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America”.

The representative Rob Bresnahan, a Republican from Pennsylvania, said in a post on social media that “an execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle”, adding that “the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment”.

“Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” he said.

On Friday of last week, the United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”, and the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the Pentagon’s plan, saying in a statement that “in no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.

“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” the statement added.

That same day, JD Vance appeared to cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution, telling reporters that “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen” when asked about the plans. The vice-president also said that if it were livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”

But over the weekend, Markwayne Mullin, who heads the Department of Homeland Security, stood behind the administration’s decision to livestream the execution.

Speaking with CBS News, Mullin said that “no one has to watch it” and said: “I follow President Trump. He’s the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job. He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he’s restoring American values.”

Trump himself had made contrasting remarks in recent days on whether the live stream would happen. On Friday, he told reporters that he “absolutely” approved the plan to livestream the execution, but on Saturday he said that he had not yet made a final decision on whether to go through with it.

“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it” he said. “’Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision.”
output.standfirst: Trump cancelled the plan to broadcast the execution after bipartisan criticism from Congress and the UN; Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, will still die by firing squad
output.progress: Trump and Hegseth agreed to drop the televised execution after bipartisan lawmakers, the UN and Catholic bishops condemned the plan.

output.headline: Jamaica secures privy council hearing date for slavery reparations case
output.bodyHtml:
A high-level United Kingdom appeals court has set a date to hear Jamaica's petition for legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations from the UK, the Jamaican government says.

Olivia Grange, Jamaica's minister of culture, says a hearing has been provisionally set for the week of 8 March 2027 by the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.

She added that the UK has until November this year to file its case.

Related: Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery

Last month, Grange led a Jamaican delegation to London to file the petition with King Charles, Jamaica's head of state. It seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.

On 23 September, Grange told Jamaica's parliament that King Charles had referred the matter to the privy council, describing the referral as a 'big deal'. She said: 'The king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the privy council, or he could make a decision to refer the questions.'

Jamaica had activated a rarely used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833, which allows the monarch to refer questions of 'legal or constitutional nature' to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts, according to the country's legal counsels.

The minister said that taking the matter to the international court of justice (ICJ) was not an option for Jamaica because the UK has placed specific reservations on the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ that prevent the court from adjudicating on disputes between the UK and the government of any other country which is or has been a member of the Commonwealth.

Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham repeated the government's long-held position that 'the UK does not and will not pay reparations'.
output.standfirst: Jamaica's minister of culture says the privy council will hear the slavery reparations petition in March 2027, with the UK given until November to file its case, despite the government's insistence it will not pay.
output.progress: Jamaica has already filed its formal petition with King Charles, seeking a ruling on whether slavery was lawful and whether Britain owes restitution.

context.text: Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged action plan with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a reparations deal, regional leaders say.

output.headline: Government funds new roads policing team to tackle cloned plates
output.bodyHtml:
The government last month said there would be a new nationwide operation against illegal number plates, with funding from the Department for Transport for a new roads policing team. A new National Roads Policing Coordination Centre would share intelligence as well as trialling new technology such as specialised goggles to detect number plates that have been designed to be unreadable by cameras.

The number of reported “cloned” vehicles involved in offences on UK roads has reached a record high, official data shows.

More than 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines for offences they said they did not recognise or accept responsibility for – most of which are believed to be down to cloning, where a number plate is copied fraudulently on similar vehicles to avoid enforcement cameras.

The number of complaints about misattribution was 9 per cent higher than in 2024 and almost double the figure recorded in 2018, according to the RAC motoring organisation, which analysed data obtained under freedom of information requests.

Related: I got £8,500 in Ulez fines after my car number plate was cloned

The RAC said the UK needed to overhaul an outdated and poorly regulated number plate system. Its head of policy, Simon Williams, said: “If number plate suppliers were carrying out all the checks they’re supposed to, it would be much harder for dodgy drivers to buy cloned plates in the first place. It’s only when a fine arrives at a vehicle keeper’s home address that they realise someone else is driving around using their vehicle’s number plate illegally.”

He said that more also needed to be done to catch drivers with ghost plates, “whether that’s more police officers being equipped with handheld devices that can detect if plates are unreadable, updating ANPR cameras and introducing higher security standards for number plates and for those who produce them”.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We’re cracking down on illegal number plates with significant investment in a new roads policing team and innovative tech to stamp out the scourge of cloned numberplates.

“Illegal number plates help facilitate crime, and we are supporting the police to work with the DVLA to make it easier to report these crimes and support victims through a new digital tool.”

Drivers using an incorrectly displayed number plate can be fined up to £1,000.

The rising figures underscore concerns about the number of illegal number plates in use, allowing criminals to evade detection and dangerous drivers to avoid being caught.

Although drivers should provide number plate suppliers with the V5C vehicle logbook and proof of identity, an investigation last year uncovered more than 130 official suppliers in the UK willing to sell cloned versions, which allow drivers to dodge police and congestion charges.

Cloning vehicles has left many innocent car owners having to struggle to prove they were not responsible when enforcement camera images apparently caught their vehicle committing offences.

A parallel concern is the use of “ghost” plates which are designed to be unreadable by the UK’s 18,000 automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) cameras, which enforce safety measures such as speed limits or lane closures on smart motorways.
output.standfirst: A new government-funded roads policing team and tech trials aim to tackle plate cloning, as the RAC calls for reform after a record 11,400 drivers were fined last year for offences not their own.
output.progress: A new National Roads Policing Coordination Centre will share intelligence and trial technology, including specialised goggles, to detect plates disguised from cameras.

output.headline: France suspends stun grenades at school protests as police officer is charged
output.bodyHtml:
Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence during school protests, and the interior minister has suspended the use of stun grenades at school demonstrations, after French lawyers and rights groups said several teenagers suffered war-like injuries from police weapons and an unprecedented number of children were held in police custody, some of whom reported being hit or racially insulted.

France is in the fourth week of its biggest youth protest movement in decades, during which hundreds of high schools across the country have been blockaded as students demand the replacement of absent teachers and repairs to decrepit buildings.

Giving evidence to the senate, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said the allegations included four children allegedly being “mutilated” by explosive weapons, and six sustaining “significant injuries”, as well as other complaints over physical blows, insults or alleged sexual assault.

Evan, a 15-year-old studying carpentry at a vocational high school, had a hand blown off in the explosion of a police stun grenade outside a school protest in Lens, northern France, on 5 October. His lawyer, Bertrand Wattez, said: “His injuries resemble war injuries.”

Wattez said Evan had gone to school to attend class and discovered a protest under way. He said Evan had not taken part in violence and denied the Béthune state prosecutor’s assertion that the grenade had been picked up from the ground. When the grenade exploded, Evan lost his left hand, several fingers from his right hand and suffered injuries to other parts of his body. He remained in hospital “in a very difficult condition” and his family had filed a criminal complaint, Wattez said.

Another boy, Eden, 14 – who had been near a school protest in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumône, north-west of Paris – suffered extensive facial injuries, including two fractures to his jaw, the loss of his bottom teeth and all his top teeth broken after he was allegedly hit by a shot from a grenade launcher.

His lawyer, Elsa Marcel, said the shot from a grenade launcher was fired at close range, from a distance of 1.5 metres. “This is the equivalent of war weaponry,” she said. The family has filed a legal complaint for attempted murder.

Eden’s parents said he had gone to school but found it blockaded and had wanted to go home. Video footage appeared to show him facing three riot police officers. One officer hit out in his direction with a truncheon and Eden kicked in the direction of the police before a grenade shot was fired. An officer has been suspended and placed under official investigation.

This week, a police officer in the western city of Tours was charged with aggravated battery after Maël, a 16-year-old at a vocational high school, lost the use of his eye allegedly after a shot from a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The officer denies the charges. The family’s lawyer said Maël had not been involved in any violent confrontation with police but had simply been present at a school protest, and that the family felt a sense of “injustice”.

For several years, France has faced scrutiny over police use of explosive weapons, particularly after serious injuries were reported during the 2018-2019 gilets jaunes (yellow vests) street demonstrations, including allegations that people had lost eyes and had their hands and feet mutilated.

The current wave of protests has also led to lawyers raising concerns that an unprecedented number of children have been arrested and placed in police custody, with some lawyers reporting that teenagers said they were hit, humiliated or verbally abused during arrests.

Since the school protests began in mid-September, a total of 6,773 under-18s have been taken into police custody after they were arrested, the justice ministry said. For more than 1,000 of those children, no charges were brought; 2,190 are facing legal action and almost 2,000 were handed an alternative to further legal action, such as a citizenship course, without their case being heard at trial and without a conviction.

Lawyers said accusations against children included gathering with violent intent, violence against police and damage to property.

Nathalie Tehio, a lawyer and the president of the French Human Rights League, said the fact that only a minority of children’s cases would end up before a judge raised concerns that arrests could be unfounded. She said: “There are a record number of arrests … Often, the legal dossiers are empty. In reality, this is more about stopping people from demonstrating. I think there is a sense of hitting hard to try to dissuade people and scare them.”

Tehio said: “We have received accounts of racist comments made. Lawyers have told us that their clients say they have been humiliated or treated violently or pushed.”

Romain Boulet, a co-president of France’s Association of Criminal Lawyers, said: “Criminal lawyers are worried and raising concerns about the potential misuse of police powers to dissuade citizens aged under 18 from demonstrating.”

Mohamed Jaite, the president of the Paris branch of the leftwing union Syndicat des Avocats de France, has represented several teenagers stopped in Paris and its suburbs. “I have seen one youth limping in a police station,” he said. “Some have reported being humiliated or receiving racist and sexist insults.”

Prisca Ancion, a lawyer from the leftwing lawyers’ group Collectif d’Action Judiciaire, which demonstrated this week in front of a high school in Saint-Denis, in the northern suburbs of Paris, said: “There have been racist insults during arrests, as well as homophobic, sexist comments or sexual touching. We encourage families to file complaints.”

Another lawyer from the collective, Romane Bartoli, who assisted several teenagers after their arrest, said: “Youngsters told us they were slapped, kicked or punched.”

Related: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state

One 16-year-old from a high school in a suburb north of Paris described being arrested 100 metres from his school on the day of a blockade in late September. He plans to study medicine at university and said he had intended to go to class before he saw there was a protest.

Answering questions from the Guardian with his lawyer, he said he had been held in police custody for more than 12 hours, mostly with two others in a police cell with two mattresses.

“It was hard psychologically because I felt I hadn’t done anything wrong,” he said. “I was hit with a truncheon and punched.”

He said a police officer told him to “shut his mouth” and said: “It’s always you lot,” which he understood to be a racist insult. He was released after a state prosecutor instructed him to carry out a citizenship course as an alternative to facing legal action.

The justice ministry and the interior ministry, which oversees policing, did not comment on allegations of insults or violence in police custody.

In parliament, Nuñez denied any form of excessive policing or police repression.

Audrey Bailleul, a magistrate and national representative of the Union Syndicale des Magistrats, said it was hard to have a clear view of events at this stage. She said: “There is nothing to show that there has voluntarily been a massive intention to not respect [legal] procedure.”
output.standfirst: The interior minister has suspended stun grenades at school protests and an officer has been charged, after four children were allegedly 'mutilated' by explosive weapons and an unprecedented number held in custody, lawyers say.
output.progress: Police have opened 36 investigations into alleged officer violence, suspended stun grenades at school protests and charged an officer with aggravated battery.

output.headline: Yemen's south rallies behind call to mobilise troops against Houthis
output.bodyHtml:
Tens of thousands of Yemenis took to the streets on Wednesday in support of a mobilisation of southern troops against the Houthis, called for by the exiled leader of the southern secessionist force, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, on Tuesday. He coupled the call with a demand for a referendum on secession within two years, and his return would be a bitter pill for Riyadh to swallow.

Yet the country’s former prime minister has said the future of western security is itself being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz.

Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.

He said: “We only have light weapons and Saudi Arabia did not plan at an early stage for this escalation, but it is never too late to regain our position.”

Appealing for more western help, Saeed said he had no doubt that the Houthis intended to seize control of all of Yemen, and claimed their goal was “to help Iran to expand the chaos”.

Saeed admitted the lack of coordination among government-backed troops, competition between Gulf states and a slowness to appreciate the implications of Yemen acquiring long-range drone technology had contributed to the pressure facing his government, and its chief backer Saudi Arabia.

Saeed called on the west to think through the implications of allowing the Houthis to take control of Yemen, arguing the country would never be secure with Houthis on the land.

Related: ‘We expect war to reach the city soon’: Yemenis stockpile as Houthis advance on Taiz

Saeed is not only an adviser to the Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, he was prime minister between 2018 and 2024 and a former negotiator with the Houthis.

He said: “The battle around Taiz is not just a battle for Taiz, but a broader battle that involves the whole of the western world, and one of the most important maritime straits. The Houthis know controlling Taiz is controlling the straits and it’s the highlands before the straits and the coastal city of Mocha and the Gulf of Aden. If Taiz is lost, access to the strait will be lost. The rest of the country will come later. The Houthi plan is to control the whole of Yemen.”

Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen after a UN-brokered ceasefire froze the frontlines in 2022.

He said existing intelligence showed the Houthis were already seeking to control parts of the south, including the former Soviet camp at al-Sabiha, in the Lahij governorate, and eventually Aden. “The Houthis bleed a lot,” he said, “they suffer a lot, but they always want quickly to use their gains or any collapse to gain more land.”

With some Houthi leaders offering safe passage to armed groups to leave the city, he said for now the Houthis were allowing some fuel and commodities into the urban area of Taiz, which houses more than 500,000 people, but in the meantime they were expanding their control of rural areas and smaller major cities.

Saeed said: “In a matter of days there will be a full siege and they will try to enter the city. I know the Houthis. They will show some flexibility until they are ready to control. It will be much worse than the siege of 2015. It will be catastrophic.”

He described Taiz as a modern democratic city untied to tribal culture, and predicted the Houthis would try to impose their Zaydi education, financial and tax systems very quickly, but the citizens would continue to resist. “The loss of Taiz would have a very significant symbolic impact on the idea of the modern state in Yemen and of resisting the Houthi project which relies on tribal networks and extremist religious education.”

Saeed admitted Taiz only had light weapons and the government had not been prepared for the loss of the west coast, allowing the Houthis to attack Taiz from four different axes.

“We have good troops,” he said, “but the problem is the coordination. We needed more communication between the National Shield Forces, National Resistance Forces and the Giants Brigades. It’s been a wake-up call inside the government and the army because not enough happened between the truce of 2022 and the restart of the fighting this year to reorganise the troops. The Houthi ideology solely is to fight.”

He added: “I hope now that the knife has come to our neck, and the Houthis represent a critical threat, the priority would be to come together to defeat the Houthis, and then to discuss other demands and guarantees.”

Saeed said it was not a coincidence that the Houthi attack along the Red Sea coast in September had come when Iran was under heavy pressure.

“Its airplanes and airports cannot operate, 90 per cent of the oil was coming out of Hormuz. That is why they attacked the Saudi east-to-west pipelines. The Houthis, by talking about a Saudi blockade, have found a reason to hit the Saudi oil installations, airports and they want to do it now because the only thing Iran can do is to keep expanding the consequences of the war for America.”

He said Houthi military capability and negotiating power had been transformed over the last decade, leading to its ability to target key sites in Saudi Arabia now. “In 2017, the Houthis had nothing but blind missiles to fire at us that missed their targets.” By 2020, he said intelligence existed that Iranian experts operating from the Houthi capital Sana’a were training Houthis, and in December of that year, in a devastatingly effective attack, they fired ballistic missiles at Aden airport. The attack left 28 dead and 107 injured, including Saeed himself, newly installed as prime minister. The missile travelled 186 miles (299km).

He explained: “We thought even then they did not have that many missiles, but since then the Iranians have expanded their manufacturing lines.” In January 2022, using missiles, the Houthis attacked Abu Dhabi oil tanker trucks more than 900 miles away.

In October 2022, inside Yemen, they struck the Nushayma oil terminal and al-Dhabba port, severely damaging government finances. By the time the US attacked Yemen in March 2025, he said “it was clear the Houthis had dozens of targeted missiles, land sea missiles and drones. They had become a unified front with Iran, and developed their missile base.”

He said: “This is a new era of radical terrorism. It is not the old chaotic one of Isis and al-Qaida. It is semi-state actors and militias threatening powerful states with cheap technologies, and smuggled third-party components. The way Iran has invested in the Houthis could become a model for threatening navigation elsewhere. It is a new model of war, without traditional armies, needing different air defences. Gulf countries have to reshape and rethink their defences.”

output.headline: Reform's own staff moved against racist candidate despite Farage's resistance
output.bodyHtml:
A senior Reform official pushed back against Nigel Farage over his handling of a racism controversy facing the party, telling him “you're protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about David Lammy, according to an undercover investigation by ITV.

Separate footage from the investigation shows Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”.

Other footage shows Farage discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party.

The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK.

Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, but the new clips from the ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who wanted the candidate sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform's head of communications, who had told another press officer that Parry was “clearly a racist”.

“He needs to go, I'm getting rid of him,” Sumner was filmed saying when the controversy broke last December. However, Parry was still the candidate three weeks later, while Farage told a press conference that the candidate could stay if he apologised.

In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said that Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate.

“He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You're protecting him.”

To laughter, Farage replied: “It's showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I'm sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he's a rear admiral. That's the problem.”

Parry was suspended on 26 March after the Guardian reported that he had described members of a Jewish neighbourhood watch group as “cosplayers” and likened them to “Islamists on horseback”.

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said these “latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform”, adding: “Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.”

The full ITV documentary, Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on Sunday, with the revelations the latest in a number of recent controversies for Reform.

Several councillors have already stood down after earlier segments from the investigation aired on Wednesday showed them making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.

Related: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and misogynist comments

The undercover reporter for ITV also met Pochin, Reform's MP for Runcorn and Helsby, at a time when she was the party's only female member of parliament.

“Oh thank fuck for that. God! We so need women press officers … They are so fucking chauvinistic,” Pochin said, after being told that a new female press officer was starting work.

“I go out on all the shows and go: ‘Oh no, it's lovely, oh they're all so welcoming.’ Shit … they just exclude you if you're a woman. It's really tough being a girl with all of this alpha male shit going on.”

Pochin did not provide a statement when approached by ITV. Reform UK, in a statement issued on Thursday, accused ITV and the company behind the documentary, Hardcash Productions, of using “extreme methods of deception”.

“They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform's headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees.

“That same journalist did not limit themselves to recording candid conversations in the workplace. That journalist also sought to find out sensitive security information, travel arrangements, and financial information outside of the scope of this investigation.”

Reform went on to say that ITV had failed to address this in correspondence, despite this conduct being drawn to its attention. “This is at a time when Nigel Farage and other members of Reform are being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation,” it added.

“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”

When approached for comment, Parry referred the Guardian to a statement given to ITV. In it he said: “I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people.”
output.standfirst: Exclusive: An ITV investigation shows Reform’s communications chief branding mayoral candidate Chris Parry a racist and demanding his removal, while Nigel Farage resisted sacking him straight away; several councillors have since quit over separate revelations, and Labour’s Bridget Phillipson says Farage must explain himself.
output.progress: Bridget Phillipson is demanding Farage explain his handling of the case, after Reform suspended Parry and several councillors resigned.

output.headline: Court hears woman's evidence as Russell Brand denies rape allegations
output.bodyHtml:
A court has heard how Russell Brand transformed into a “monster” when he allegedly made a woman take half-naked photographs of him before raping her in a hotel room at a Labour party conference.

The 51-year-old comedian denies attacking the woman, who told Southwark crown court, breaking down in tears in the witness box, that she could not fight him off.

“He was really heavy,” she said. “I couldn’t struggle. I couldn’t breathe. I know he raped me, I know I said: ‘No, no, I don’t want this.’”

Brand, who denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009.

Brand fixed his gaze on one of the TV screens in court on Thursday morning as a video of the woman’s interview from 27 September 2023 was played. She told police she met Brand at a fringe cabaret event that he was performing in during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She was not attracted to the then unknown performer, whom she assumed was gay and who showered her with compliments.

But she found him polite and intelligent, and the pair spoke about their work before going back to her hotel room to continue their conversation.

The woman said she “froze” in the run-down single room when she returned from the toilet to find that Brand was partly naked and “prancing around” like an ostrich. She said she asked him why he had undressed, and he told her: “Don’t worry, I’m mostly naked at home.”

The woman told how she became “frightened” when Brand made her take half-naked photographs of him. “I took pictures of him on my camera – he made me take them,” she said. “I remember feeling: ‘What on earth have I got myself into?’”

She told police he then raped her in an attack that lasted up to 10 minutes and left her feeling scared, in pain, and as if she couldn’t breathe.

“He did rape, he did push me on the bed,” she told police. “He did pull my clothes off, he took my trousers off.

“I remember him on me, very heavy. I know I said no. I kind of drifted out of my head. I couldn’t get out of the situation – ‘do I shout, do I scream?’ He was very heavy, I couldn’t breathe, it didn’t take long.”

She described his body as snake-like and “disgusting” and said his tongue was “horrible” like a lizard. “I’m saying ‘no, no’ but I was really scared,” she told police. “I know he groped me. I know he was touching me, I know he grabbed my breasts. I know he tried to kiss me and I moved my neck. I didn’t want his mouth on mine.

“He was just pulling my trousers down and pulling my underwear off, and he was inside me. It was not nice, it was painful and it hurt.”

Giving evidence from behind a screen in the afternoon, the woman added: “I was like a zombie on the bed. All I could think was he’s inside me and the quicker the better.”

In tense exchanges during cross-examination with the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, the woman denied that Brand had persuaded her to have sex. “He was frightening, he seemed menacing at that point,” she replied. “He’s scary. I didn’t know what to do.”

She rejected Winter’s suggestion that she had fallen under the spell of Brand, whom the barrister described as charismatic with a magnetic personality. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, had to interrupt the lawyer during one exchange to object to one of his questions, saying: “Shush please. I’m the judge, you have to let me talk.”

The woman told the court Brand was a “completely different persona” in the hotel room. When pressed further by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones, the woman said: “He just changed suddenly from camp, friendly and effeminate to monster-like.

“I felt very scared in that moment. He was big, I felt threatened and he’s half naked. And while I’m naive, I didn’t think at that moment his intentions were good.

“He was just dark and arrogant and performing – he was scary, he was demanding. He was the centre of the show, it was like it was back on stage – he wasn’t the [same] person I was chatting to.”

The woman told police she closed her eyes during the attack and that Brand made her feel sick and dirty. She recalled: “He was making noises, a lot of noises of enjoyment and saying how pretty I was. I remember him complimenting me, saying: ‘Are you enjoying it’? I remember him asking me. Obviously I didn’t answer.”

She alleged that Brand spoke as the attack was unfolding. She told police: “He was just saying: ‘We’re having fun, it’s fine, it’s all good, don’t worry about it, it’s just fun, it’s normal.’”

The woman, who had been a victim of abuse in the past, said Brand made her compare earlier experiences, and it “stuck in her head … is this what abusers do?”

She told police: “It was almost like to convince me it’s all OK and that I’d enjoy it, that I’d have to learn to enjoy it.”

In the aftermath, she said Brand acted “like nothing was wrong”, wrote down his email address, and suggested that his mother might like to meet her.

She told the court: “He is so arrogant in his mindset that he’s God’s gift that I must’ve enjoyed it and I must’ve wanted more.”

The following morning, she banged her head against the wall because she felt numb. She told police she had had nightmares about being pregnant and said she kept quiet about the incident for years as she watched Brand becoming “more and more famous”.

The woman said a 2023 Dispatches documentary about allegations of sexual misconduct by Brand “triggered” her to go to police.

Brand denies the allegations. The trial continues.
